projects.title: Global Consulting Challange: Champions
projects.description:
USC Marshall MBA students won the Overall Challenge and Company Segment of the 2016 Global Consulting Challenge, held March 3-4 at Google, Inc. headquarters in Mountain View. The five-member case competition team created a plan to transform the internal audit process, which has direct applicability to every internal audit department today, through use of data analytics.

"As the faculty adviser for the team, I am pleased to report that our students offered a big, bold and sophisticated platform,” said Suh-Pyng Ku, vice dean for graduate programs and professor of clinical finance and business economics. “Effectively, they built a rocket ship."

“I know I speak for the entire team when I say that the GCC was the most difficult and rewarding part of our business school experience,” said Michael Kohl MBA ’17, who served as team captain. “Everyone from our professors to our classmates to the MBA program staff contributed to this victory. We could not have done this without the support of our Trojan family.”

The Global Consulting Challenge is a 14-year-old invitation-only case competition that draws teams from leading business schools around the globe. It is usually held at USC's University Park Campus. This year, however, Google invited USC Marshall to host the competition at its campus.

Teams had three weeks to delve into complex, hypothetical data sets from Google and prepare presentations for three judging panels. Teams did not reveal their school affiliations until after the judging.

USC Marshall was one of nine teams competing. Participating business schools included Chicago Booth, Copenhagen Business School, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), IESE, MIT Sloan, Northwestern Kellogg, NYU Stern and Yale.

headline: Deals Partner @ PwC | Simplifies the Complex | People & Value Focused | Servant Leader | Board Member | Avid Cyclist
about:
I bring over 20 years of experience helping my clients transform their organizations and connect value and human capital within the context of a transaction -- acquisition, divestiture, carveouts, etc.  I have broad expertise encompassing HR, culture, change management, communications, talent management & retention, and leadership alignment across both private equity and corporate clients and the industrial products & services, Energy, and Power and Utilities industries. 

My reputation, however, is based on my ability to equip and empower my teams with the right tools and techniques that liberate existing organizational intelligence, insight, wisdom and talent. 

As a change champion, I believe in the thought shared by Dr. Travis Bradberry: “Managers light a fire under people. Leaders light a fire in people.” Leading by example is the surest way to building trusting relationships and creating a picture of what's possible. 

The greatness of a community is proportional to the compassionate actions of its members. As a servant leader, I've dedicated the last 20 years of my career to helping underserved and underrepresented communities. An opportunity to serve people that look like me (Black, women, and youth) is a non-negotiable. Guided by passion, resilience, and commitment, I gain immense satisfaction in standing in the gap of opportunity and hard work, connecting the dots for other community members.

experience.description:
While Black businesses and the community currently have some resources and opportunities, they tend to be scarcely known or publicized. The opportunities that are known tend to be inaccessible and fail to meet business owners where they are. This could be due to any number of reasons such as resource location in the city or the level of difficulty required for the application process. This is where we come in!

Revitalize Black Chicago (RBC) is a 501(c)(3) focused initiative led by African American community leaders and residents to restore historically Black neighborhoods stifled by years of disinvestment, disenfranchisement, and economic instability.

Three key areas of specialization:
 
✔ Small Business Support 
✔ Workforce Development
✔ Financial Literacy

Taking the helm as the co-founder, I revitalize Black Chicago with a focus on grassroots initiative that seeks to meet our communities where they are, restore a sense of pride, and expand the foothold of those who have already seen some success individually or as a business.

For more inquiries, connect with me here on LinkedIn or visit: www.revitalizeblackchicago.org

headline: Director, Mergers and Acquisitions Tax at PwC
about:
I am a Director in PwC’s M&A Tax practice in Chicago, IL, but based in Houston, TX. As a member of the M&A Tax team, I help our clients with various aspects of merger and acquisition transactions, such as restructuring, divestitures, and partnerships. Specifically, I manage multiple tax structuring and tax due diligence projects related to domestic and cross-border transactions for strategic and financial clients, including buy-side and sell-side tax due diligence across various industries. This includes but is not limited to tax attribute planning, stock basis analyses, earnings and profits computations, NOL utilization planning, and reviewing the tax aspects of relevant transaction documents such as sale and purchase agreements.

A part of my role includes managing multiple local teams and specialty teams throughout the tax structuring and tax due diligence process and communicating with clients on various tax issues and potential tax reduction strategies and solutions.

In addition to my role as a M&A Tax professional, I am a pillar leader within the Deals Council of Black and Latinx professionals within PwC. I also function as a formal and informal coach to a number of our professionals and interns.

headline: Transformation Senior Manager at PwC
about:
Carolyn has a diverse background in client service, Human Capital, Resource Management and Operational roles, as well as transformational projects. She has helped both internal and external clients navigate through changing environments.  

Carolyn is a Senior Manager currently working on a National Transformation team. Carolyn's Resource Management expertise, knowledge and understanding of business needs and attention to detail helped drive the development and successful rollout of PwC's first global operating platform. 

Carolyn started her career at PwC as part of the Core Attest practice serving public and private companies in the Consumer & Industrial Products and Services industry.  Even in client service, Carolyn was very involved in the firm's People strategy, therefore it was an easy transition for her to move from client service into an HR Manager role, followed by a Staffing & Deployment role, followed by an Operations role and eventually into her current Transformation role.

experience.description: What started as US focused process improvement project has grown into a firm-wide global talent transformation project.  My initial role on this project was to provide resource management and deployment expertise to the team as we worked through our current state assessment and future state vision of Resource Management.  My role has now grown into a Functional Design Manager, responsible for identifying and documenting the business requirements of our new Resource Management tool. My work over the last several years has included conducting various focus groups and usability sessions to further refine our requirements, strong collaboration with other internal groups within PwC (including IT, Change Management & Communications, Learning & Development), global stakeholder management and most recently user acceptance testing as we prepare to rollout our new solution.

Portfolio Manager (PoM) supporting multiple Core Attest market  teams  in Greater Chicago; The PoM role was a combination of deployment & operations.    I was responsible for strategic deployment (~200 professionals and ~75 clients) and internal business processes/operational matters.  The latter included the following types of activities: monitoring of billing and collection efforts, WIP review, annual budgeting process (headcount and hours), monthly projections, internal compliance tracking, team and market reporting, Regional Finance requests,  and prep and facilitation of monthly Manager meetings and quarterly market team meetings.

In November 2013, our resource management & operations organization modified our roles into pure deployment or operations roles and I moved into the Operations Manager role supporting all 5 Core Attest market teams in Greater Chicago.  My responsibilities no longer included deployment activities, but my operations role now expanded to the full Attest practice.

I provided HR support to roughly 120 audit professionals.  I worked directly with our team's Partner Leader to roll out and implement the Firm's Human Capital strategy to our team.  My responsibilities included daily coaching of staff, performance management - including driving the annual review process for my team, compensation planning, headcount forecasting, coordination and facilitation of quarterly team meetings.

Provided assurance services to a variety of clients, including those in the industrial products and services sector.  My clients ranged from small private domestics companies to large publicly traded international companies.  Over my years of experience I moved from simply executing test plans to developing and implementing the audit approach, including test plans for the design and operating effectiveness of internal controls.  Planning efforts also included personnel planning, budgeting and forecasting.  My responsibilities also included testing of complex accounting areas to ensure proper application of accounting standards.  Other key areas of focus were on staff coaching & development, as well as overall project management.

volunteering.description:
Onward provides social services to low-income families in Chicago’s Belmont Cragin neighborhood and the surrounding areas.  Onward provides services ranging from Pre-K and Head Start programs for young children, youth programs and tutoring services for school age children, adult English as a Second Language (ESL) and computer literacy programs, as well as support to seniors through the Onward Friendship Club.  Onward also operates a food pantry that works in partnership with the Greater Chicago Food Depository to buy and distribute foods at no cost to families and individuals residing in Chicago.  Onward’s unifying philosophy is one of family support, aiming to build the strengths and assets of its families by involving them as community partners and leaders. Onward directs its many services towards working families and individuals of low income status.

The Auxiliary Board's (AB) primary mission is to help raise funds for the organization.  We host a charity gala every winter, which is our primary fund raiser. I served as the Fundraising & Auction items (Silent & Live auction) Chair from 2010 - 2015 and also served as the AB President in 2011 & 2012.

projects.title: A Symmetric Key Cryptosystem using Transcendental Numbers
projects.description:
This project was done as my final year B.E dissertation. Around the time I started this project, vulnerabilities of AES cipher were exposed, and many blogs were being written on it. 
My project was to extend Rijndael Cipher (AES) and make it more secure by fixing the vulnerabilities in same computational time.

I observed that the decimal expansion of Transcendental numbers are completely random. By exploiting this mathematical phenomenon, the S-Box in AES was randomised after each round. My algorithm builds new S-Box at the end of each round and encrypts the data.

Finally the Transcendental number, decimal place from which S-box was randomised and a private key are used in the new algorithm, which takes the security of AES cipher to whole new level.

slides.title: Light up someone’s world: Encouraging others to use cameras during virtual meetings
slides.subtitle: Daniel Walker CP APMP on LinkedIn
slides.description: One unforeseen consequence of the new way of working is the expectation that we’re all joining virtual meetings. No matter where we are, or how many meetings we’ve joined in the past, they’re always stressful. If you’re anything like me, I’m always wondering, “Will I look alright? What if my pets appear in the background? What if I need to get up in the middle of a call?” These are all valid questions, but to make sure you and others get the most out of your meeting, it's important to stay visible and appear engaged. Here are a few tips to help you use your camera and encourage others to do so. Set a trend: Join the call a few minutes early and turn your camera on. As others join, they’ll see your example and be encouraged to do the same. Use introductions creatively: Many people are afraid to turn cameras on because they’re embarrassed about their backgrounds. To remedy this, tell your participants what they might see in the background as an introduction. For example: “Hi, I’m Daniel, and today you might see my guitar behind me, I’ve been a terrible player since high school.” Then repeat the exercise with others--this will put them at ease with what’s behind them and set a conversational tone for the rest of the meeting Acknowledge the fact you’re at home, and you can’t control what’s happening. As with the background example, set a tone for this with everyone upfront in an introduction. For example: “Hi, I’m Daniel, I’m expecting a package from Amazon any minute, so please forgive me if you hear a doorbell and puppies barking.” Set the tone for your meeting by acknowledging the elephant in the room: that you're at home and can't control what's happening around you. For longer meetings, use spotters: A spotter is a member of your team who monitors a meeting and reports who’s paying attention, or who’s off camera to presenters and facilitators. If you know of 2-3 critical audience members, have your spotter pay close attention to them, and send you updates of what they’re doing in an offline chat. Then, as appropriate, call on them, or conduct an energizer exercise to bring the group together if they’re tuning out. Match your tone: Put your audience at ease by showing you're in a similar situation to them, and that you understand their challenges by matching your style and expectations to what's possible for them. Research your audience and determine their individual circumstances. For example, if you know someone has small children at home, don't pressure them to be on camera. Accordingly, try to match your clothing, accessories, and appearance to your audience. In an example, if you know your primary participants are casual, wear less formal clothing. Look, sound, feel your best: Nothing will engender confidence like knowing you’ve done all you can do to look and sound you best on camera. Invest in a high quality webcam and microphone. Don't rely on your built in laptop devices. When it’s time to be on screen, try to place your face in the center of the shot. This will help minimize the appearance that you’re towering over the screen, and show that you’re engaged and ready to listen. Show you’re interested: It’s disheartening to see others not paying attention. Do all you can to combat this by keeping your eyes on the camera, and not multitasking. Make eye contact with the camera at all times. It may be tempting to look at your participants as you speak, but doing so will make your eyes shift. Instead, place your eyes on your camera, and try not to look away when you’re speaking. Rely on your spotter to monitor the virtual room and give you feedback. Likewise, when a critical audience member is speaking, or you’re being addressed, look into the camera. This shows you’re engaged, and tells their spotter that you’re a VIP. Finally, while we all adjust to a new way of working it’s entirely natural to feel uncomfortable with these ways of connecting. However, remember, it’s entirely likely your audience feels the same way. So don't be afraid to smile, to laugh, and to try new things. After all, we’re all in this together, and in doing so, you might just bond with your audience in new ways.

slides.title: Keeping Control: Managing Virtual Meetings
slides.subtitle: Daniel Walker CP APMP on LinkedIn
slides.description: Earlier this week we explored some general ideas about working, and managing projects, from home. A huge part of this is managing virtual meetings, calls, and teleconferences. In over 10 years, I’ve led more virtual collaborations than I can count, working with professionals from 6 continents. It’s not always easy, but here are some ideas to help: Get your tech ready All of these tips mean nothing if you can’t connect to the office. Be sure your laptop and phone are charged up, your VPN is working, and your teams have a strong collaboration space. Also test out microphones before meetings, making sure you don’t have too much background noise, and try out your camera keeping an eye on how you look, and also what’s in the background. Speak slowly and enunciate Keep in mind your audience might be outside, or surrounded by noise. Make sure everyone can clearly understand you at all times by talking slower than a normal conversation, and projecting your voice, even if it’s just into a headset. Stay visible If possible, share your screen and use your camera during virtual meetings, this helps others get a sense of who you are, and also keeps them focused on the items being presented. Share an agenda, and ask questions in advance Keeping a virtual meeting in order starts by sharing the reason for why it’s happening in the first place. Make sure every meeting has a clear agenda, with speaking roles mapped to each agenda item. Share this well in advance of each meeting, and again 10-15 minutes before the meeting if practical. This helps keep teams focused, and also helps you end detailed conversations that could be taken offline. Come to virtual meetings with an overly positive attitude TV anchors are told to exaggerate their emotions; the same is true for anyone on a virtual meeting. The tone you set as the leader of a virtual meeting generally determines its outcome. Arrive at each call early, prepared with an agenda, and with an overly positive attitude. Your colleagues can’t see you, so all they have to go by is the tone of your voice. Staying upbeat will motivate them, and help keep them focused. Hold daily team meetings, even for 15 minutes Not everyone is going to be engaged on every project every day, but you don’t want them to forget your project. Set aside a daily touchpoint with your colleagues, if only to say “good morning.” People are more likely to ask questions on the phone than take the time to write an e-mail. Your quick time to ask how things are going can mean the difference between a project moving along, or falling behind. At the same time, it helps your team feel engaged, and establishes you as a leader who’s interested in their success and the project’s objectives, helping them realize they can come to you with concerns. Take roll, or use a tool that does it for you It’s critical to make sure you have the right audience, and that others are aware of who’s with them on a call. At the onset of each call, ask all attendees to announce themselves, and run down this list before getting started. This not only helps others feel included, it positions you as the first speaker, letting you control the agenda. Use a tracker Since you can’t look across the room, or pop into a colleague’s office to check on status, it’s critical to stay on top of action items. Building a tracker to monitor progress is an excellent way to stay organized. Using a spreadsheet, start by listing all RFP requirements, assigning an owner, due date, and keeping a running list of notes related to each line. You can also add in lines for other open items, but ensure all items are tied back to some measure of customer compliance and responsiveness. This is another great place to consolidate your writer’s sheets and client hot button issues, as specified by APMP. Prioritize meeting items For virtual meetings, timing and scope creep are productivity killers. Since you can’t read the room, you can’t easily control what happens. Combat this by sending an agenda for each meeting, and following it to the letter. When reviewing progress on a document, don’t share the draft Many times a virtual review session is derailed because one person isn’t happy with the color of a graphic, or the font in a particular section. Combat this scope creep by only sharing your tracker on your screen during meetings, and encouraging your team to follow along in the document on their own screens. This helps them focus only on what’s required at that moment, while minimizing the risk of your call descending into chaos. Be clear with follow up items, and over communicate After each meeting, share follow up items immediately, and ensure all follow up asks clearly specify timing, ownership, and escalation pathways. At the same time, remember that teams generally respond better to simple tasks with short deadlines. This helps empower a team to understand what’s expected of them, and helps them think of potential bottlenecks or areas where they may require additional support. While virtual meetings have never been called easy, they don’t have to be painful. Taking the time to plan ahead will help empower your teams, and make you an e-meeting superstar in no time. Want to learn more about managing proposals, and how to get the most out of your team? Follow me on LinkedIn and check out my latest book, Preparing for a Shift: How Millennials will Redefine the Proposal Industry on Amazon

slides.title: The New Normal: Adjusting to Managing Proposals From Anywhere
slides.subtitle: Daniel Walker CP APMP on LinkedIn
slides.description: As humans, we’re social animals. The need to connect is hardwired into each of us. For those of us in the bid and proposal industry, this drive for connection is even stronger. Think of all the bonds that are made in a war room, all the nuance that goes into driving a team towards successfully building a complex bid. Now try to do this without the benefit of seeing your colleagues face to face. It’s a hard skill to master, but one we’ve learned. I’ve supported thousands of bids, working remotely for over 10 years. With all of us working virtually for at least a few weeks, here are some practical ideas to help you get the most out of your teams while you can’t be in the office. Set clearly defined start and end times The hardest part about working from home is managing your time. Believe it or not, it’s not getting motivated that’s tough, it’s quitting at the end of the day. While at the office you can walk out the door and leave your work for tomorrow, this isn’t possible when working from home. To fight burnout, try to start your day at roughly the same time every morning, and set a clear end time for when you’ll walk away from your computer. Keep rituals alive Staying plugged in and motivated comes from maintaining what worked well for you in the office. If you start every day with a danish and coffee from the corner bakery, have the same breakfast in your kitchen before going heads down into work. Create a separate work space At the end of a stressful day, isn’t it nice to walk out of the office and leave that part of your life behind you? To the extent possible do the same when working from home. Try to set up a separate room, or a place in your home that’s only dedicated to work, and do as much of your work there as possible. Also, tell your kids and significant other to keep their distance from this space, as you need to be fully engaged during work hours. This not only keeps you focused by minimizing distractions, but it also keeps work turmoil from becoming a part of your home and limits the impact of your being there to your family. Respect boundaries Boundaries not only apply to how you handle working from home, but how you interact with others who are doing the same. As mentioned above, start by dedicating as separate a space as you’re able to be your dedicated workstation. Have discussions with your family or those who live with you about your working hours, and establish times when you’re not to be disturbed. Share the outcomes of these conversations with your leadership and teams, and ask the same of them. By setting boundaries up front, you set expectations, minimizing the chances of confusion and last minute crises. For example, if you need to make dinner for your kids from 4PM - 6PM every day, communicate to your teams that you’ll be offline at this time during kickoff, and discuss coverage options. Make time away from work Whatever you do, don’t let work bury you, and don’t isolate. To the extent it’s currently possible, maintain your normal work hours, and take time to keep on doing the things you’d normally do. Get away from your desk between meetings, and get outside as much as you can. Staying active is critical to keeping your motivation levels high. Control your own calendar To the extent you can, set your own invites when you're working from home. While you need to respect your customer’s needs, doing this for non essential or internal meetings helps minimize the chance you’ll be working off hours. Also, carefully evaluate how long you need meetings to last. Many times, what takes an hour in person can be done in 30 minutes on the phone by sharing materials and asking questions in advance. Make time to connect, and find new ways to do it Time with your colleagues doesn’t have to be all work and no play, Find ways to stay connected, and share in each other's lives. Some ideas include starting a book club, and having a video conference session to discuss what you’ve read, or hosting a video watch party on social media. Also, send work anniversary and birthday notes, and be sure to recognize any successes virtually just like you’d do in the office. Get your tech ready All of these tips mean nothing if you can’t connect to the office. Be sure your laptop and phone are charged up, your VPN is working, and your teams have a strong collaboration space. Also test out microphones before meetings, making sure you don’t have too much background noise, and try out your camera keeping an eye on how you look, and also what’s in the background. Practice self care Working from home is hard. This might be the first time in decades you’ve been asked to do this, and it’s ok if it feels overwhelming. Nobody is perfect at this, and we will all learn from the progress we’re making. But look at each day as an opportunity to work from home a little bit better, and understand that many others are in the same place as you are right now. Enjoy the flexibility Want to have lunch at 11AM on your patio? Feel like walking the dog when the sun’s out at 3 in the afternoon. Go ahead! It’s ok to step away if you’re caught up. Make the most of this time and take care of things you would have never done at the office. Just make sure you’re prioritizing work, have the right approvals, and take your phone with you. In the end, working from home can be as exciting as it is gratifying. Just be sure to set clear boundaries and expectations, communicate with your colleagues, and take care of yourself along the way. You may find this new way of working is just right for you! Want to learn more about managing proposals, and how to get the most out of your team? Follow me on LinkedIn and check out my latest book, Preparing for a Shift: How Millennials will Redefine the Proposal Industry on Amazon

headline: Deals Manager at PwC, CPA
about:
✦ Summary ✦

A CPA with 7+ years of client-facing experience at PwC, I’ve supported both private equity and corporate clients across financial due diligence and audit engagements. My background spans financial due diligence analysis, audit execution, and cross-functional collaboration across a range of industries and business models. I’ve worked with companies ranging from early-stage growth to large multinational corporations—each presenting its own set of financial structures, operating models, and complexities.

I began my career in PwC’s Audit and Assurance group, where I led audit work for Fortune 500 clients in the automotive, consumer products, and business services sectors. That experience built a strong foundation in technical accounting, internal controls, and financial statement risk assessment. Since transitioning into PwC’s Deals practice, I’ve supported over 20 buy-side and sell-side transactions across manufacturing, technology, and healthcare. My work focuses on helping clients assess the quality of earnings, understand working capital and debt-like items, and identify key risks and performance drivers to inform investment decisions.

In my current role as a Manager in the Financial Due Diligence team, I lead engagements from kickoff through delivery, coordinate closely with cross-functional teams, and support senior stakeholders throughout the diligence process. I enjoy navigating the complexity of financial data, drawing insights that bring clarity to the deal process, and helping clients move forward with confidence.

✦ Key Achievements ✦

▸ Led and supported 20+ financial due diligence engagements for private equity and corporate clients, involving businesses with EBITDA ranging from under $100K to over $200M
▸ Managed cross-functional workstreams (including tax, HR, and operations) and led daily communication with internal and external stakeholders
▸ Reviewed earnings and net working capital analyses, normalized financial results, and prepared client deliverables including databooks and executive-ready reports
▸ Gained experience across a range of sectors including manufacturing, consumer products, technology, healthcare, and business services

Please feel free to contact me at cunhamorrie@gmail.com.

headline: Manager - Consulting at PwC
about:
I am currently an Manager in the Operations Consting practice at PwC with a focus in the Digital Solutions group, primarily servicing clients in the Insurance sector. 

Since joining this practice in Jan 2018, I have advised large life and annuity providers through multi-year digital transformation programs by providing program management, change management, program governance, business analysis, data analytics, quality assurance and support. 

Prior to Jan 2018, I spent a year in PwC’s Deals practice advising clients through complex financial reporting issues arising from both sell-side and buy-side transactions in the insurance space, see below for notable experiences. 

In Dec 2016, I graduated with High Distinction from the Tippie College of Business at The University of Iowa with majors in Finance and Accounting. 

Prior to graduation, I interned at PricewaterhouseCoopers as a Deals Summer Associate, working in the Capital Markets & Accounting Advisory vertical. I gained experience performing due diligence for supplier financing and receivable factoring arrangements, as well as, providing SEC-compliant comfort for a public senior note offering. publications.title: Fabrication of Micro-Batteries via Stop-Flow Lithography
publications.description: Fabrication of micro-MEM devices and stretchable wearable electronics is important for future applications in materials, medicine and drug delivery. A key challenge in this area is the fabrication of rechargeable micro batteries with thicknesses < 500 μm, area < 0.1 mm2, energy densities of at least 1 to 10μWh cm-2 μμm-1. The overarching aim of this project is to develop a robust platform to fabricate micro batteries by combining double emulsion generation to fabricate porous microspheres that will serve as the anode and cathode materials and stop-flow lithography in microfludic devices to assemble the battery internals in a single step. In this presentation, I will discuss the tasks performed to assemble the stop flow lithography system, and the generation of active materials from double emulsions. The tasks include: (1) setting up the shutter and solenoid as well as syncing their operation, (2) fabricated masks for micro-particles by electric cutter and printing method, (3) performed trials to fabricate particles of different sizes and shapes, and (4) fabricated and operated double emulsion devices. The work accomplished during the summer serves as a strong foundation for the rest of the project.

Marty Collins is a Partner in PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP Washington National Tax Services Office.   In his role, Marty works with client service teams for several of the Firm's premier clients as an international tax partner.

Marty's practice covers a wide-range of cross-border tax issues, including analyzing developments and identifying planning opportunities arising from new tax legislation (2017 Tax Reform), regulations and treaties.  Much of Marty’s work emanates from his clients’ acquisitions, dispositions or business expansions.
 
Marty specializes in advising clients on structuring tax-efficient acquisition and disposition structures, cross-border reorganizations including section 7874 (inversion) considerations, inbound financing structures, cross-border joint ventures, and principal/entrepreneur structures.  Marty's practice includes developing and analyzing strategies for tax-efficient IP, financing and holding-company structures, including strategies for the redeployment of foreign earnings.  Marty regularly advises clients on the U.S. anti-deferral (e.g., Subpart F income and GILTI), overall foreign loss, and foreign tax credit rules and regulations.

Marty frequently speaks and writes on a broad range of international tax issues.

Marty joined PricewaterhouseCoopers in 1995 in Baltimore; transferred to Washington National Tax Services from 1998 to 2003; transferred to Chicago from 2003 to 2005; and then rejoined in March 2008 from McDermott Will & Emery where he was a partner in that firm’s tax practice from 2005-2008.

headline: International Tax Manager at PricewaterhouseCoopers
about:
I have worked in international tax services at PwC since receiving a full-time offer while at Ohio State University. I work with a variety of teams, both internal and external to PwC, on projects covering general international tax concepts, technical international tax concepts, mergers & acquisitions, and transfer pricing. I have a wide breadth of coverage in these subject matter areas, in addition to experience working with other tax, accounting, and financial matters.

I have experience acting in a manager capacity where I have team(s) working under my supervision and have been afforded extensive opportunities to work in a project-manager capacity, with cross-functional teams outside of tax.

My client base has been diverse and I have a working knowledge of the pharmaceutical, biomedical, and industrial and specialized manufacturing industries, along with a moderate level of experience working with private equity clients.

Beyond the skills I've acquired while working as an international tax professional at PwC, I have a robust level of knowledge and interest in the sports industry. I have demonstrated an ability both within my career as a tax professional and outside of it that I have an affinity for innovation and finding new ways to add value and create efficiencies. These examples are prevalent in my career where routine tasks on various projects I've worked on have been automated or reimagined in order to optimize resource deployment.

The vast majority of my career has been spent on team-based engagements where I collaborate with upper-management and lower-staff levels and have been responsible for communicating project findings, results, and presentations in client-facing environments and for high-level, industry-wide, partner-facing meetings and summits.

Overall, I've shown capabilities in performing within a team-setting and managing both the people that work under my supervision, and also perform under the supervision of those those above me. Given the breadth of my diverse client-base and projects I've had the opportunity to work on, I have a tremendous understanding of different working styles and industries and can be flexible in adapting to any environment I find myself. I have lived overseas and have an appreciation for both work and non-work cultures across the globe, which has only been elevated due to my career in international tax. As an employee in a public accounting space, I've gained a healthy understanding of the quality of work that's necessary to succeed in a professional environment and am always willing to go the extra mile

projects.title: Deception Detection using Machine Learning
projects.description: This dissertation describes work on deception detection in text, speech and video using machine learning techniques. Deception detection has been a study of interest in various domains like forensics, psychology, computer science and linguistics. It has promising applications in real life as the human counterparts are poor at detecting lies. This work examines the ability to deceive for different types of questions: Leading questions and open-ended questions, positive assumptions and negative assumption questions, outcome and process questions, recollection and hypothetical questions. This dissertation shows that video processing techniques and speech processing techniques can be applied to the domain of deception to extract useful features for classification. We also looked at the personality factors using the big five personality test and checked its impact on deception detection ability. An important product of this work is a balanced video and audio data set simulating a job interview. Results show that supervised classification models like K nearest neighbours classifier and support vector classifier can classify text and audio data to some success: The accuracy is better than human hearers and chance. Long short-term machines are used to classify the video data after facial feature extraction leading to test accuracy of 64.7%.

slides.title: It’s Time to Step Up
slides.subtitle: Nikki H. on LinkedIn
slides.description: I honestly wasn’t sure how to start this blog. How do I put into words the impact that Shane has made on my life, who I am as a person, and as an ally? How do I capture everything that Shane means to me, as a sibling, as a friend, and as the big brother that I will always admire? I’ll start with this. Shane was born 16 weeks premature. He spent the first six months of his life in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU), surrounded by nurses, doctors, and my parents fighting for his life. My older brother spent the first six months of his life fighting harder than most of us have fought in our lives. Shane has the mental capacity of an eight-year-old, but he has more determination, more joy, more excitement, more curiosity, and more love than any adult I know. Shane has Cerebral Palsy, but he is not defined by Cerebral Palsy. Cerebral Palsy essentially is a condition that affects normal movements in different parts of the body. ‘Cerebral’ refers to the brain’s cerebrum, the part of the brain that controls our motor functions. ‘Palsy’ describes the paralysis of different muscles and voluntary movements of the body. This is often accompanied by cognitive impairment and delays in motor skills. Cerebral Palsy differs in type and severity for each and every person — and there is no way to know the type and severity that each individual has without learning about it first-hand. And that’s why this cause means so much to me. As a young girl, I remember being out in public, at the park, the pool, even the grocery store, and feeling other children’s eyes on my family. Their eyes were focused on Shane, a young boy in a wheelchair who did not look the same as them, and it infuriated me. Why were these kids and their parents staring at my older brother with fear in their eyes and why would they just stare? If they were going to stare, why wouldn’t they come say hi or interact with us? Shane has a smile on his face almost all the time, it’s not as though he’s intimidating or mean. In fact, he is the nicest, happiest, most caring person that I know, yet these strangers couldn’t see that. They couldn’t see that or understand that because they didn’t try. They didn’t ask. It wasn’t until many years later that I understood that these children and their parents didn’t have foul intentions, they just simply did not know how to understand, how to try, or how to interact with my brother. I’m here to tell you that it can be simple. The first step is to stop staring and wondering, and to interact with Shane like you would anyone else. Ask him his name, what he likes, how he’s doing, what he wants to do, what music he likes — basically any question you would ask anyone else to get to know them. Then you learn through interaction, and you learn through understanding that he is a 30 year old man who has had to face more obstacles than most in his life. Your interactions with Shane may be different than those with another 30 year old man, but you should approach them similarly. He will answer your questions and ask you questions of his own. His favorite question that he asks people is ‘Is your phone fully charged?’ — he will ask our waiter or waitress at a restaurant, the grocery store clerk ringing us up, he asks me every time I talk with him —this is essentially his way of asking how you’re doing. He grew up in the era where everyone was attached to their smartphones, and heard everyone always worrying about their phone being dead or needing a charger, and essentially understood this as a question for him to relate to others. Shane has his own cell phone and he loves to talk on that thing, so it better never have low battery. If you really want to make his day? Ask him if he wants to vacuum — his absolute favorite thing to do. My brother wakes up every morning, blasts his music, and starts the day jamming in his bed. He wakes up every morning excited to be alive and excited to spend time with friends and family. Regardless of all that Shane has been through in his life, including battling cancer, this man radiates more positivity than anyone I know ever could. I am happy that PwC has given me the opportunity to have a voice and to share my brother's incredible story. I’m grateful to be a part of an organization that is participating first-hand in raising awareness and funds for Cerebral Palsy. I’m also grateful for a firm that cares, and that wants to make an impact on not only their employees’ lives and employees' loved ones, but also make an impact on the world. STEPtember is one of the many ways that PwC is doing so. So please, step up for #TeamShane. Step up for those who cannot step up themselves. Step up because Shane is a blessing in this world and it’s time for everyone to understand that Cerebral Palsy does not define a person. It’s time for us to step up to continue funding the cutting edge research around Cerebral Palsy, to educate others and to educate ourselves. Getting started is as easy as this: Download the STEPtember App Visit http://www.steptember.us/join/pricewaterhousecooperspwc to register individually or as a four-person team, and to learn more about STEPtember If you aren't interested in participating yourself, please feel free to donate to #TeamShane here.
